blocks.content: Imagine you move apartments and forget to tell anyone your new address. Your friends still show up at the old place, knock on a stranger's door, and leave confused.

That is basically what happens to a service in a microservices system every time it restarts, scales up, or gets redeployed to a new machine. Its network address changes, and every other service that had that address hardcoded is now knocking on a stranger's door.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304075-814621345.png
blocks.alt: A hardcoded IP address becomes invalid after a redeploy, causing connection refused errors

blocks.content: Service discovery is the system that keeps everyone's address book up to date automatically, so nobody has to remember a phone number that changed last night.
Service discovery is the mechanism by which one service finds the current network location, host and port, of another service instance, without anyone hardcoding an IP address anywhere.

It sounds like a small problem until you actually run more than a handful of service instances. Then it becomes one of the first things you have to solve, before load balancing, before circuit breakers, before almost anything else.
1. Introduction
In a monolith, this problem barely exists. Your code calls a function in the same process. There is no network hop, so there is nothing to discover.

Break that monolith into services and everything changes. Now the order service needs to call the payment service over the network, and the payment service might be running as three instances, five instances, or fifty, depending on the time of day.

["Autoscaling adds and removes instances constantly based on load, so the set of valid addresses is never fixed for long.","Deploys replace old instances with new ones on new machines, so an address that worked an hour ago might point at nothing now.","Crashes remove instances without warning, and a container scheduler usually starts a replacement somewhere else entirely."]
items: Autoscaling adds and removes instances constantly based on load, so the set of valid addresses is never fixed for long.
Deploys replace old instances with new ones on new machines, so an address that worked an hour ago might point at nothing now.
Crashes remove instances without warning, and a container scheduler usually starts a replacement somewhere else entirely.

blocks.content: Hardcoding an IP address in a config file works fine for a demo. It falls apart the moment instances become disposable, which is exactly what happens in a containerized, autoscaled world.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304076-105000566.png
blocks.alt: Multiple payment service instances registering their current location with a central service registry

blocks.content: The fix is a service registry, a live directory of who is currently running and where. Every instance tells the registry it exists when it starts, and the registry is the one place everyone else checks before making a call.

blocks.title: Why this matters early
blocks.content: You cannot design a system with more than one instance of a service without answering this question. That is why service discovery shows up in almost every microservices interview, even when the interviewer never says the words out loud.

There are two broad ways to use that registry once it exists: the caller can talk to it directly, or something in the middle can talk to it on the caller's behalf. Those are client side discovery and server side discovery, and the rest of this topic walks through both.
2. Client side discovery
In client side discovery, the calling service does the work itself. It asks the registry directly, gets back a list of healthy instances, and picks one using its own load balancing logic.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304076-726103240.png
blocks.alt: Client queries the registry directly then calls the chosen instance

blocks.content: 2.1 How it works

["The order service asks the registry a simple question: who is currently running the payment service.","The registry replies with a list of addresses, for example three IPs and ports for three healthy payment instances.","The order service picks one, often with a simple strategy like round robin or random choice, and calls it directly."]
items: The order service asks the registry a simple question: who is currently running the payment service.
The registry replies with a list of addresses, for example three IPs and ports for three healthy payment instances.
The order service picks one, often with a simple strategy like round robin or random choice, and calls it directly.

blocks.content: Nothing sits between the caller and the callee once the address is chosen. The registry is only consulted for the lookup, not for every single request.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: The calling service now needs a discovery client library baked in. Every language your services are written in needs that library, or its own equivalent, kept in sync with how the registry works.
2.2 Netflix Eureka in practice
Eureka is the classic example of this pattern, popularized by Netflix and widely used in Spring Cloud based systems. Each instance runs a small Eureka client alongside it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306365-946313657.png
blocks.alt: A payment instance sends heartbeats to Eureka while the order service fetches the cached registry

blocks.content: On startup, the payment instance registers itself with the Eureka server. From then on it sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds or so to prove it is still alive. The order service periodically pulls a fresh copy of the registry and caches it locally, so a lookup never has to leave the process on the hot path.
That local cache is the whole point. Even if the Eureka server goes down for a minute, the order service keeps working off its last known good list of instances instead of failing every request.
3. Server side discovery

Server side discovery moves the lookup out of the caller entirely. The caller just calls a fixed, well known address, and something else, usually a load balancer or router, looks up the registry and forwards the request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306367-305502417.png
blocks.alt: A router looks up the registry on the caller's behalf and forwards the request to an instance

blocks.content: 3.1 How it works

["The order service calls a stable address, for example payment-service, and never touches the registry itself.","A router or load balancer in front of the payment service intercepts that call.","The router checks the registry, picks a healthy instance, and forwards the request there."]
items: The order service calls a stable address, for example payment-service, and never touches the registry itself.
A router or load balancer in front of the payment service intercepts that call.
The router checks the registry, picks a healthy instance, and forwards the request there.

blocks.content: The calling service does not need any discovery logic at all. It just makes an ordinary network call and lets the infrastructure figure out where that call actually needs to go.
3.2 Kubernetes Services and kube proxy

This is exactly how Kubernetes handles service to service calls. A Kubernetes Service gives you a stable virtual IP and DNS name, even though the actual pods behind it are constantly being created and destroyed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306368-765169799.png
blocks.alt: An order pod calls the payment Kubernetes Service, which kube proxy routes to a healthy payment pod

blocks.content: kube proxy runs on every node and maintains routing rules, usually backed by iptables or IPVS, that send traffic for that virtual IP to one of the current pod IPs behind it. The pod list itself comes from the Kubernetes API server, which is the registry in this picture.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If you draw a Kubernetes Service in a system design interview, you are already implicitly using server side discovery. It is worth saying that out loud, it shows the interviewer you understand what the abstraction is doing under the hood.
4. Client side vs server side discovery
blocks.text: 4. Client side vs server side discovery

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306369-205261078.png
blocks.alt: Client side caller queries the registry directly, server side caller lets a router query the registry

blocks.content: Neither approach is universally better. The right choice depends on how much control you want the caller to have versus how much you want to push into shared infrastructure.

{"headers":["Client side discovery","Server side discovery"],"rows":[["Caller talks to the registry directly","Caller never touches the registry"],["Needs a discovery client library per language","Works the same for every language, since it is just a normal network call"],["One less network hop per request","Extra hop through a router or load balancer"],["Load balancing logic lives in every client","Load balancing logic lives in one central place"],["Example: Netflix Eureka with Ribbon","Example: Kubernetes Services with kube proxy"]]}
A lot of teams end up on server side discovery today simply because Kubernetes gives it to them for free. You do not have to write a discovery client, you just call a Service name.
5. Service registration
None of this works unless instances actually show up in the registry in the first place. That process is called registration, and it happens the moment an instance is ready to take traffic.
5.1 Self registration

The simplest approach: the instance registers itself. On startup, it calls the registry's API and says here I am, this is my host and port. On shutdown, it calls the registry again and says take me out.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306369-153261639.png
blocks.alt: A new instance calls the register API on startup, which adds it to the service registry

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Self registration only works if shutdown is graceful. A hard crash never runs that deregister call, which is exactly why health checks exist, covered next.
5.2 Third party registration

The alternative keeps registration logic out of your application code entirely. A separate registrar, often a sidecar process or a piece of platform infrastructure, watches for new instances and registers them on the application's behalf.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306370-545614552.png
blocks.alt: Kubernetes detects a new pod and a registrar sidecar registers it in the service registry

blocks.content: Kubernetes itself is a good example. Your application never calls any registration API. The kubelet reports the pod as ready, and the Kubernetes control plane updates the Service's endpoint list automatically.

This is less code for you to maintain, but it also means the registration logic lives entirely in infrastructure you do not control directly. If it has a bug, every service on the platform inherits it.
6. Health checks and deregistration
A registry that only removes entries when instances politely shut down is not good enough, because instances also crash, freeze, or get network partitioned without ever saying goodbye.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306370-60107904.png
blocks.alt: The registry pings an instance, gets no response, and removes it from the registry

blocks.content: That is what health checks are for. The registry, or an agent working for it, regularly pings every registered instance. Miss enough pings in a row and the instance gets marked unhealthy and pulled out of the pool, even if it never called deregister itself.

["Active checks the registry actively hits an endpoint like /health on a timer and expects a quick 200 back.","Passive checks the registry watches for repeated call failures against an instance and evicts it after a threshold.","Heartbeats the instance pushes a keep alive signal to the registry, and missing a few in a row triggers eviction."]
items: Active checks the registry actively hits an endpoint like /health on a timer and expects a quick 200 back.
Passive checks the registry watches for repeated call failures against an instance and evicts it after a threshold.
Heartbeats the instance pushes a keep alive signal to the registry, and missing a few in a row triggers eviction.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Without health checks, a client side discovery cache can keep handing out the address of a dead instance for minutes. Every request to it fails, retries make it worse, and users feel it as slow, flaky responses instead of one clean error.

Health checks are also how a slow but technically alive instance gets treated. Some systems mark an instance degraded rather than just up or down, and steer less traffic to it instead of cutting it off completely.
7. Real systems
You rarely build a service registry from scratch. A handful of well tested systems cover almost every case you will run into.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306371-622072590.png
blocks.alt: Service discovery landscape covering Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes DNS, and etcd

blocks.content: 7.1 Consul
HashiCorp Consul is a general purpose service registry with built in health checking, a key value store, and support for both client side and server side patterns through its DNS and HTTP interfaces.
7.2 Eureka
Netflix's Eureka is the classic client side discovery registry, built for an AWS environment where instances came and went constantly and DNS based approaches were too slow to keep up.
7.3 Kubernetes DNS
Kubernetes gives every Service a DNS name automatically. Calling http://payment-service resolves through the cluster's internal DNS to a stable virtual IP, which kube proxy then routes to a real pod.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306371-299859388.png
blocks.alt: CoreDNS resolves the payment service name to a pod IP inside the cluster

blocks.content:
# From inside any pod in the cluster
curl http://payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local/charge

# CoreDNS resolves payment-service to the Service's cluster IP,
# kube proxy then forwards to one of the healthy backing pods

code.content:
# From inside any pod in the cluster
curl http://payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local/charge

# CoreDNS resolves payment-service to the Service's cluster IP,
# kube proxy then forwards to one of the healthy backing pods

blocks.content: 7.4 etcd

etcd is a distributed key value store, not a service discovery system on its own, but it is the storage layer underneath both Kubernetes itself and plenty of custom built registries. It is what makes the registry data consistent and durable across a cluster.

8. Worked example: order service calls payment service
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: order service calls payment service

blocks.content: Say the order service needs to charge a customer. It has three payment service instances registered, but one of them has been failing health checks for the last minute.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396306371-295719456.png
blocks.alt: Order service queries the registry, one unhealthy instance is excluded, two healthy instances remain

blocks.title: Order service discovering payment service
blocks.text: Three payment instances exist. Instance C stopped responding to health checks two minutes ago and was marked unhealthy. The order service asks the registry for healthy instances only, gets back A and B, and picks one to call.

blocks.content: Instance C never enters the picture because it already got filtered out at the registry lookup step. If the order service had cached a stale list from ten minutes ago, it would have wasted a request, a timeout, and a retry just to find that out the hard way.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Discovery only helps if the caller actually uses the fresh list. A cache that refreshes too slowly, or a hardcoded fallback address left over from testing, quietly reintroduces the exact problem service discovery was supposed to solve.
9. The interview angle

Service discovery rarely gets asked about as its own standalone question. It shows up the moment you draw more than one instance of any service in a design, which is almost every real system design interview.

["The moment you draw two boxes for the same service, an interviewer can reasonably ask how one finds the other.","Naming client side versus server side discovery, and picking one with a reason, signals you understand the tradeoff instead of just drawing boxes and arrows.","Mentioning health checks shows you have thought about what happens when an instance dies, not just the happy path."]
items: The moment you draw two boxes for the same service, an interviewer can reasonably ask how one finds the other.
Naming client side versus server side discovery, and picking one with a reason, signals you understand the tradeoff instead of just drawing boxes and arrows.
Mentioning health checks shows you have thought about what happens when an instance dies, not just the happy path.

blocks.title: How to bring it up
blocks.content: If you are already using Kubernetes in your design, just say so: "the Service and kube proxy handle discovery here." That is a complete, correct answer and takes ten seconds to say.
You do not need to reimplement Eureka on a whiteboard. You need to show that you know discovery is a real problem, name the two patterns, and pick the one that fits the rest of your design.
10. Key takeaways

["Instances move around constantly in a microservices system, so hardcoded addresses break almost immediately.","A service registry is the live directory of who is running and where, kept fresh by registration and health checks.","Client side discovery puts the lookup and the choice in the caller, server side discovery hides both behind a router.","Instances register themselves on startup, or a third party registrar does it on their behalf.","Health checks are what actually keep the registry honest when instances crash instead of shutting down cleanly.","Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes DNS, and etcd cover almost every real system you will encounter or design around."]
items: Instances move around constantly in a microservices system, so hardcoded addresses break almost immediately.
A service registry is the live directory of who is running and where, kept fresh by registration and health checks.
Client side discovery puts the lookup and the choice in the caller, server side discovery hides both behind a router.
Instances register themselves on startup, or a third party registrar does it on their behalf.
Health checks are what actually keep the registry honest when instances crash instead of shutting down cleanly.
Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes DNS, and etcd cover almost every real system you will encounter or design around.

blocks.content: Wherever you draw more than one instance of a service in a design, service discovery is quietly the thing making the arrow between boxes actually work.
